html:
The Myaamia, or Miami, are an Algonquian-speaking Native American people of the western Great Lakes. The map places them in 1492 across what is now Indiana and nearby parts of Illinois, Michigan and Ohio. Their language, Miami-Illinois, was shared with the Illinois to the west.

They lived in river villages, growing maize, beans and squash, and hunted deer and bison on the prairies. During the Beaver Wars of the 1600s, raids by the Haudenosaunee drove them west for a time. They came back to the Wabash and Maumee rivers, where their main town, Kekionga, stood on the site of today's Fort Wayne. Later snapshots of the map show them simply as the Miami.

In the 1790s their war leader Little Turtle helped defeat two American armies, the second at St. Clair's Defeat in 1791. The Americans won at Fallen Timbers in 1794, and treaties then took most of their land. In 1846 most Miami were removed to Kansas, and later to Oklahoma; some stayed in Indiana. The Miami Tribe of Oklahoma has since revived the language, which had lost its last native speakers in the mid 1900s.
